Condition: MID

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
There is a particular kind of quiet that settles over an old atlas. If you open one printed thirty or forty years ago, the spine cracks with a dry, papery sigh, and the colors bleed slightly past their borders—pale ochre deserts, bruised-violet mountain ranges, and oceans tinted the faded cyan of swimming pools at the end of August. On those pages, the world feels simultaneously vast and containable, folded neatly into linen-bound boards. You can trace a finger along the jagged coast of Chile or let your palm rest over the entire expanse of the Siberian steppe, feeling the slight grit of ink on pulp. What strikes me most about these artifacts is not their accuracy—borders shift, coastlines erode, and cities swell past their printed dots—but their generosity toward the unknown. Even in the late twentieth century, an atlas left room for the imagination. A thin blue line labeled simply *seasonal river* or a cluster of unnamed islands off a northern archipelago functioned as quiet invitations, whispering that the world had not yet been entirely chewed over and swallowed by certainty.

Contrast that with the maps we keep in our pockets today. Our digital cartography is a marvel of utility, an endless, frictionless scroll of satellite imagery stitched together without seam or shadow. With two fingers, you can plummet from the curvature of the earth straight down into the parking lot of a suburban strip mall, close enough to count the oil stains on the asphalt and distinguish a Subaru from a Honda. There is no *terra incognita* left on the surface, no polite blank spaces where a cartographer might have sketched a sea monster out of sheer boredom or honest ignorance. Everything is rendered in crisp, midday brightness. Yet in gaining this omniscience, we lost a subtle kind of scale. When every alley in Lisbon and every gravel turnoff in Montana appears at the exact same resolution, distance loses its weight. We forget what it feels like to wonder what sits behind a ridge, because we have already rotated the terrain model on glass before packing our bags.

Perhaps that is why I find myself drawn to the cartography of memory—a map that refuses to stay proportional. In the geography of recall, scale is governed by emotion rather than kilometers. The block where you grew up might measure four hundred paces from corner to corner, yet in your mind, it remains a continent. There was the hollow beneath the cedar hedge where the dirt stayed cool in July, the tilted sidewalk slab lifted by an ambitious maple root that launched bicycle tires into brief, terrifying flight, and the corner store whose screen door slammed with a metallic clack announcing summer. Return to those streets years later, and the proportions collapse with almost comical abruptness. The daunting hill becomes a mild incline; the dense woods behind the schoolyard reveal themselves as a scrubby strip of trees barely deep enough to hide a parked truck. It feels like a minor betrayal, as though someone shrank the scenery overnight, when in truth it was only your attention that used to magnify the world.

We also carry a collection of phantom geographies—places we have never stepped foot in, yet know with strange intimacy. Think of the towns seen only from the window of a night train or the elevated curve of an interstate overpass. You pass through in seven seconds flat, just long enough to register a brick water tower, a row of clapboard houses with peeling porch paint, and a single yellow kitchen window glowing against the indigo dusk. Inside that frame, someone is standing at a sink, reaching into a cupboard, or leaning over a table with their chin in their palm. You will never know their name or the sound of their voice, yet that fleeting image lodges inside your head like a pressed flower. These unvisited places possess a clarity real destinations rarely keep once you arrive and have to look for parking. Unburdened by logistics, they remain pure possibility—a whole novel you didn't have to finish writing.

When the physical map runs out of mystery, human curiosity simply migrates elsewhere. We turn our compasses downward into deep ocean trenches where sunlight has never touched the silt, inward into the tangled, electric forest of the nervous system, or outward toward faint smudges of ancient light gathered by mirrors floating in the dark. Yet even in ordinary days, uncharted territory persists in the small silences we usually rush to fill. Sit on a park bench for twenty minutes without reaching for a phone, and the familiar geometry of an afternoon begins to shift. You notice the weird, deliberate choreography of pigeons, the way wind ripples through a stand of sycamores in delayed waves—first the high crown, then the middle boughs, then dry leaves skittering along the bench legs—and the layered hum of a city breathing. These are not places you can pin with coordinates, yet they are landscapes all the same, waiting just beneath the threshold of habitual distraction.

Maybe the real art of wandering now is learning how to leave parts of your own life unmapped. We live in an era that rewards exhaustive documentation: every meal photographed, every trail logged by satellites, every stray thought polished into a neat little pebble and tossed into the public stream. There is a quiet rebellion in choosing not to record a moment—in walking down an unfamiliar street purely to see where it bends, without checking the blue dot pulsing on a screen, and letting the memory of it stay slightly blurry around the edges. Let the river remain seasonal. Let a few northern islands go unnamed. A good map tells you how to reach your destination, certainly, and there is comfort in knowing the route, but a full life still needs margins left wide and blank, waiting for whatever unscheduled weather decides to blow across the page. After all, the territory is always larger than the paper, and the best discoveries remain unmarked.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical, sensory essay develops a distinctive meditation on maps, memory, and the value of leaving room for uncertainty.

## Grounded reading
The voice is contemplative and warmly nostalgic, but not simply anti-technology: it admires digital maps’ utility while mourning how their completeness can flatten distance and wonder. Its pathos comes through in small, tactile scenes—the cracked atlas spine, the childhood hill that shrinks with age, a stranger’s lit kitchen glimpsed from a train. The essay invites the reader to slow down, attend to what usually goes unnoticed, and let some experiences remain unrecorded or unresolved.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds old atlases, blank spaces, childhood landscapes, fleeting views of strangers, and ordinary city sounds as sites of possibility. It gives moral weight to curiosity, unhurried attention, and privacy, suggesting that a life need not be exhaustively mapped or documented to be fully lived.

## Evidence line
> What strikes me most about these artifacts is not their accuracy—borders shift, coastlines erode, and cities swell past their printed dots—but their generosity toward the unknown.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sustained map metaphor, vivid sensory details, and repeated defense of mystery and unrecorded experience make this a distinctive, coherent expression of those concerns.
